name: Conjunctivitis
definition: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin clear membrane that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.
overview: Conjunctivitis, often called pink eye, is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin clear tissue that covers the white of the eye and lines the eyelids. It is a common condition that leaves the surface of the eye red and sore, and often sticky or watery. The NHS describes three kinds: bacterial, viral and allergic. Most cases get better on their own, and most people do not need antibiotics even when bacteria are the cause.
causes: Viruses, usually those behind colds and flu (viral conjunctivitis)
An allergic reaction to things such as dust, grass or pollen (allergic conjunctivitis), often linked to hay fever
Chlamydia infection, which the NHS says may lead to referral to a sexual health clinic
riskFactors: Close contact with someone who has infective conjunctivitis, because it spreads on hands, towels and washcloths
signs: A watery red eye in viral conjunctivitis
A red eye with a sticky yellow discharge in bacterial conjunctivitis
Swollen eyelids and stringy discharge in allergic conjunctivitis
Widened blood vessels in the white of the eye in allergic conjunctivitis
complications: Viral conjunctivitis can last two to three weeks even with the correct treatment
Some sight-threatening eye conditions can look like conjunctivitis
Trachoma, which first appears as inflammation of the eyelid lining (conjunctivitis)
diagnosis: The sources describe the types mainly by how the eye looks and by the pattern of symptoms. Viral conjunctivitis tends to cause a watery red eye, while bacterial conjunctivitis is more likely to cause a sticky yellow discharge. NICE has published a briefing on a point-of-care test for diagnosing adenoviral conjunctivitis.
treatment: Most cases get better on their own. Home care includes cleaning crusts from the eyelids with cooled boiled water, using a cold compress and avoiding contact lenses until the eyes are better. Antibiotics are not effective against viral or allergic conjunctivitis, and antihistamines can ease allergic symptoms. A pharmacist can advise on eye drops or antihistamines.
prevention: Frequent handwashing and proper disposal of tissues are advised for viral conjunctivitis. Towels, pillows, eye drops and make-up are not shared until the discharge has cleared.
seekCare: NHS 111 or a GP the same day is the route for eye pain, sensitivity to light, changes in vision or a very red eye, which the NHS says can be signs of a more serious eye problem. Moorfields advises contacting Moorfields Direct or going to a local A&E if vision becomes more blurred, eye pain becomes noticeable or blisters or spots appear on the eyelids. A newborn baby with a red or sticky eye needs to be seen urgently, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day. A routine GP appointment is the usual route if symptoms have not cleared within about a week.

sections.heading: What is conjunctivitis?
sections.body:
Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva, the thin clear membrane that covers the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids. Many people know it as pink eye. It is a common condition that leaves the surface of the eye red and sore, and the eye is often sticky or watery. The NHS describes three kinds of conjunctivitis: bacterial, viral and allergic.

Bacterial and viral forms are together known as infective conjunctivitis. Infective conjunctivitis is usually caused by bacteria or by the viruses behind colds and flu. Allergic conjunctivitis is a reaction to things such as dust, grass or pollen. The NHS links the allergic kind with hay fever and says it makes the eyes red and watery but is not contagious.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of conjunctivitis?
sections.body:
The NHS describes red, sore, itchy and watery eyes, often with a sticky discharge. The eyes may feel gritty, and the eyelids may be stuck together in the morning. The type of conjunctivitis tends to change how the eye looks.

Viral conjunctivitis tends to cause a watery red eye. Bacterial conjunctivitis is more likely to cause a red eye with a sticky yellow discharge. Allergic conjunctivitis can bring red, itchy, watery eyes, sore eyes and swollen eyelids. Blurry vision can happen in the allergic kind because of the excess tears. MedlinePlus also lists stringy discharge and widened blood vessels in the white of the eye for allergic conjunctivitis. Sources differ on whether the discharge looks like pus or is watery, and this tends to depend on the cause.

sections.heading: How is conjunctivitis diagnosed?
sections.body:
The sources describe the types mainly by how the eye looks and by the pattern of symptoms. Viral cases tend to give a watery red eye, while bacterial cases are more likely to give a sticky yellow discharge. NICE has published a briefing on a point-of-care test for diagnosing adenoviral conjunctivitis.

Some sight-threatening eye conditions can look like conjunctivitis, which is why clinicians look for warning features. The NHS lists eye pain, sensitivity to light and changes in vision such as wavy lines or flashing as signs of a more serious eye problem. A chlamydial form of conjunctivitis may lead to referral to a sexual health clinic. Trachoma, a different eye infection, first appears as inflammation of the lining of the eyelids.

sections.heading: How is conjunctivitis treated?
sections.body:
Most cases get better on their own. Moorfields says most infections clear up within a few days to a few weeks. The NHS says most people with conjunctivitis do not need antibiotics, even when bacteria are the cause. Antibiotics do not work if the cause is a virus or an allergy.

Home care described by the NHS includes cleaning crusts from the eyelids with cooled boiled water and using a cold compress. Lubricating drops, sometimes called artificial tears, can ease grittiness but do not shorten the illness, according to Moorfields. The Moorfields leaflet says paracetamol or ibuprofen can help with discomfort. Antihistamines can ease the symptoms of allergic conjunctivitis. A pharmacist can advise on eye drops or antihistamines. Moorfields notes that steroid eye drops are occasionally used in severe cases.

sections.heading: How does conjunctivitis spread, and can it be prevented?
sections.body:
Viral conjunctivitis is contagious, and Moorfields advises frequent handwashing and proper disposal of tissues. One NHS leaflet says conjunctivitis is usually spread by direct contact, on hands, towels and washcloths, and by droplets coughed or sneezed into the air. NHS leaflets advise against sharing towels and pillows, and suggest washing bedding and face cloths in hot water. Another NHS source adds that eye drops and make-up should not be shared until the discharge has cleared.

Allergic conjunctivitis is not contagious. Moorfields says contact lenses should not be worn until symptoms have cleared completely. Most NHS guidance says children do not need to stay off school or nursery, although families may be asked to keep a child at home when there is a cluster of cases. Moorfields has a children's page that lists separate towels and staying off school until better as family advice.

sections.heading: When should you get medical help for conjunctivitis?
sections.body:
Most conjunctivitis does not need urgent care, and Moorfields lists allergic conjunctivitis as not an emergency. The NHS says eye pain, sensitivity to light, changes in vision or a very red eye need urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day. These can be signs of a more serious eye problem, the NHS says.

The Moorfields leaflet says to contact Moorfields Direct or go to a local A&E if vision becomes more blurred, eye pain becomes noticeable or blisters or spots appear on the eyelids. A newborn baby with a red or sticky eye needs to be seen urgently, through NHS 111 or the GP the same day. A GP appointment is the usual route if symptoms have not cleared within about a week. For children, the NHS advises seeing a GP if there is no improvement after two weeks. A contact lens wearer who has spots on the eyelids is advised to see a GP.

faqs.a: Infective conjunctivitis can spread from person to person, mainly on hands, towels and washcloths. Moorfields describes viral conjunctivitis as contagious and advises frequent handwashing. Allergic conjunctivitis, such as the kind linked to hay fever, is not contagious.

faqs.q: Do people with conjunctivitis need antibiotics?
faqs.a: The NHS says most people with conjunctivitis do not need antibiotics, even when bacteria are the cause. Antibiotics do not work against a virus or an allergy. Moorfields says antibiotic drops are generally not effective against viral cases. Whether eye drops are prescribed for a particular person is a decision for the clinician or pharmacist who sees the eye.

Moorfields says most infections clear up on their own within a few days to a few weeks. Viral conjunctivitis can last two to three weeks even with the correct treatment. An NHS source says many cases clear within one to two weeks, and often within two to five days. In children, the NHS advises seeing a GP if there is no improvement after two weeks.

faqs.q: Can contact lenses be worn with conjunctivitis?
faqs.a: The NHS advises against wearing contact lenses until the eyes are better. Moorfields says they should not be worn until symptoms have cleared completely. One NHS source adds that lenses should stay out for 24 hours after symptoms have gone. A contact lens wearer who has spots on the eyelids is advised to see a GP.

faqs.q: Does a child with conjunctivitis need to stay off school?
faqs.a: Most NHS guidance says children do not need to stay away from school or nursery. The exception is a cluster of cases, when families may be asked to keep a child at home until the infection has cleared. Moorfields has a children's page that lists staying off school until better among its family advice, so advice varies. Separate towels and handwashing are the main advice.
